children: By Steve Garmhausen

Most accounting firms that add wealth management to their services want to keep it. After big accounting and consulting players Moss Adams and Baker Tilly merged last year, they decided to spin theirs off. Justin Fisher, the head of the wealth business — now called Threadline Wealth — says potential conflicts of interest and a need for focus were big factors. "One cool thing about our spinout is that we did it in such a collaborative way with the accounting firm," says Fisher, whose business is based in Bellevue, Wash. "We sat down together, looked at all these factors, had a strategic discussion and said, 'That makes the most sense; we should operationally separate the RIA.' "

Speaking with Barron's Advisor, Fisher, who leads a nearly $6 billion-asset business with 65 team members, discusses the process of breaking away. He explains why one big center of influence isn't enough. And he argues that, the spinoff notwithstanding, there's a big opportunity in coordinating clients' wealth and accounting needs.

Threadline was spun off from Baker Tilly early this year. Why did that make strategic sense for all the parties? You've got to focus on what you want to be great at from a strategic perspective. And it's fair that a large-scale accounting firm like Baker Tilly or Moss Adams has to put all their strategic horsepower into being the best, in this case, middle-market global accounting and advisory firm they can be. And on the wealth management side, you understand the competitive landscape there. You've got to have 100% of your board meeting focused on that.

So it was really an open and honest discussion on strategic priorities. Like, is this going to make a board agenda? Is this going to be a meaningful component of our strategy or not? I think the answer is that for a large accounting firm like Moss Adams and Baker Tilly, it's not.

The other consideration is that independence becomes a real conflict. We work with business owners, founders, and executives — qualified purchasers that are often having private investment exposure. As they sell their business, they become liquid. They want to get back to being illiquid in some portion of their allocation. Well, if we're trying to put a venture fund into a portfolio that fits well for that client's investment goals and objectives, our accounting firm might be auditing that fund right now. So we literally have a conflict of interest where we're wanting to do great work from an accounting standpoint with this fund; we know it's the best fit for the portfolio, but we can't do it because we have an independence conflict. That doesn't make sense for the client. Those two things were the two fundamental considerations there.

And then the big practical questions arise. First and foremost, how do you navigate funding the spinoff? One cool thing about our spinout is that we did it in such a collaborative way with the accounting firm. We sat down together, looked at all these factors, had a strategic discussion and said, "That makes the most sense; we should operationally separate the RIA."

So then we asked, "Should the RIA go to a strategic partner, some larger firm, or does the RIA have enough capabilities to be independent?" We looked at both of those options. We talked to strategic partners. We looked at what it would take operationally to spin out as an independent business. We concluded that, based on the scale of the RIA and its capabilities we'd be fine spinning off separately.

So then it was about finding a capital partner with the right expertise and long-term view that is going to help the RIA thrive over a long period. We hired an investment banker and interviewed several firms, and ended up selecting the Cynosure Group. They've been in wealth management for a long time and have a long-term nature to the work they do. It was a good match for creating value long term.

Describe the identity of Threadline. Our vision is to reimagine advisory coordination to create better outcomes for clients. Our mission is around working with the CPA community to create outcomes that drive value for owners, founders, and executives.

We like to have fun. We like to prepare. We're relentless in improving. We're really curious. We're a group that's generally on the younger side, that wants to grow and dive into that client mission around the CPA and wealth communities. We'd been inside an accounting firm for so long that it's really core to who we are. A lot of our advisors are CPAs, for example.

As far as your sales model, you have an obvious center of influence with Moss Adams, and maybe because you're independent of them now, other accounting firms are comfortable working with you as well. Can you talk about your pipeline? Most wealth managers think of accounting firms as tax folks, but they're really audit, tax and consulting, and advisory. So first and foremost, when we're interacting with a CPA, we want to understand who are they serving and what problem they are trying to solve for the client. What do they really do, and how can we be a partner to help them find new clients and better serve clients?

We have advisors specializing in working with the CPA community for different sectors like food, beverage, and agribusiness in the San Joaquin Valley, as an example. These are advisor teams that are very familiar with fruit growers and things like that, and understand the economic models for those businesses, so that they can add value working with CPAs that work with those types of businesses.

Then there's the other side of the spectrum, with the tech community in Silicon Valley. The CPA community in the Bay area has a partner in Threadline that adds value for them as they serve their clients, with advisors who are very well versed in executive compensation, stock planning, these kinds of things. It's much less about having a CPA refer us work and much more about trying to understand how we can click into that CPA to create value for client situations.

And we send a lot of work over to the CPA side, as you would imagine. We're out in the community connecting with owners and executives, and we often hear about service gaps, whether it's audit, tax, or advisory. And it's easy to make an introduction to our accounting counterparts. That's core to our ethos because we've been embedded in that ecosystem for so long.

The referral pipeline between Threadline and Baker Tilly — is that enough for now, or are there other accounting COIs as well? Baker Tilly is certainly a thriving accounting firm. Their private-client practice is special, so there's a ton of opportunity to work together. With that said, Baker Tilly isn't the best fit for certain clients' situations. We do work with other CPA firms as well. And when I talk to my colleagues at the Baker Tilly side, they don't worry about that. We naturally end up interacting with other CPA firms based on client fit, just like they could tell they will interact with other wealth firms for client fit.

It does seem like there's a gap between wealth management and accounting for many clients, and thus an opportunity for both professions. I think so too. We work with business owners, executives, founders, qualified purchaser-type clients. I believe they need more accounting advice as we go forward, not less. I'm watching their tax situations become more complex as their businesses become more complex, multistate, global, these kinds of things, so the accounting is a major part of that client's experience, which then becomes a major part of that client's wealth outcomes.

So certainly there's this gap to fill there. To do that, you've got to really meet the accounting community where it's at and help fill gaps of client experience. We can do little things like create agendas multiple weeks in advance for client meetings and help prepare for those meetings — these kinds of things. We can get dashboards into the hands of tax preparers so they have an early heads up around potential gains and losses in private investments.

When I talk to my friends in the accounting community, they're often trying to pull information out of the wealth community, and they might not know that the wealth management team met with the client three times recently or whatever it might be. Some of those things seem silly, but both communities are trying to do their best work, and what happens is we'll do our best work independently and forget that coordination layer that creates so much value for clients. So I do think there's an awesome opportunity there.

What have been one or two of the most complicated challenges of spinning off into an independent business? When you have a business that's been intertwined within another for 20 years, there are a lot of shared services, legal and HR, some really important business backbone components that you will lose access to. Those things are anticipated, but nonetheless, they're challenges. Some of the things that are a bit unanticipated include some of the complexity around deal structure: making sure you're putting together a structure that works well for both sides. When you've been so integrated it takes a lot of financial accounting work to determine where does this business [accounting] end and where does this one [wealth management] start. Even just creating a banking relationship: It might be surprising how complex that is and how important it is to find a banking partner that really understands your business and understands the mission and vision that you have.

There are also a lot of great things that our previous firm did. Firms like Baker Tilly and Moss Adams are long-term successful firms for a reason. Some of the things that were amazing about those firms, such as their ability to communicate a very clear and concise strategic document, that creates a lot of value and it's really hard to do. Those are things you don't need to change, so you should be able to grab some of the components that made that firm successful. So when you're spinning out from a firm that's been very successful, don't try and re-create the wheel.

Looking ahead five years, what do you hope that your biggest quantifiable accomplishments will be? Culture to me is always the No. 1 thing about our business. So having net promoter scores and cultural aspects that show we are creating a unique firm that is a supportive home for those in the wealth community in the age of AI. We want to have metrics around being an amazing place to work, grow your career, and build your skills and talent. On the client coordination side, it would be having a certain number of clients that have both a CPA and us as a wealth partner, and perhaps a legal or other professional advisor that we have a strategic relationship with. I would want that number of our clients to be in the 90% range. Those things would result in our expansion geographically, which would result in us becoming a bigger firm — $20 billion, $30 billion, that kind of thing.
Thanks, Justin.
